strengths: Well-motivated and clearly defined problem: quantifying 'local routing consistency' of MoE models is directly relevant to expert offloading systems, and prior work (e.g., Mixtral observations, Eliseev & Mazur) only examined short spans on single models without systematic treatment.

Two complementary metrics (SRP and SCH) are carefully formalized, with derivations and proofs in the appendix showing they are intrinsic properties of experts/models and how the optimal segment router/cache is characterized. The connection between the two metrics is empirically validated (high correlation, Table 7).

Broad and valuable empirical coverage: 20 MoE LLMs spanning 3B–57B, diverse architectures (dense-layer skipping, shared experts, encoder-decoder, SSM hybrids), a mixed corpus covering generic and downstream domains, and 8x RTX 4090 hardware makes the study accessible and reproducible.

Actionable findings: (a) MoE-on-every-layer + no shared experts correlates with highest consistency; (b) domain-specialized experts contribute more than vocabulary-specialized ones; (c) cache size ~2x active experts balances effectiveness/efficiency. These are useful for both MoE architecture design and offloading system configuration.

Good empirical hygiene: base vs. post-trained comparison, position-wise SRP analysis, bootstrapped confidence intervals (Table 8), correlation with real cache algorithms (LRU/LFU/Fixed, Table 3), and controls for perplexity and other architecture parameters.
Reproducibility is addressed: deterministic corpus construction, promised release of code and sampled corpus.
weaknesses: Primarily an observational study with no end-to-end validation: the paper never demonstrates that higher SRP/SCH translates into actual inference speedups or quality retention in a real expert-offloading system; the link to practice rests only on hit-rate correlations with cache algorithms, and the 'ρ=2' recommendation is derived from oracle (SCH) turning points rather than measured latency/throughput trade-offs.

Key architectural claims are correlational and confounded: the 'MoE on every layer + no shared experts' observation comes from comparing 20 heterogeneous models differing in size, training data, and objectives. Group 1 and Group 2 share these traits yet differ substantially in SRP (78.16 vs ~49), so the stated conditions are at best necessary, not sufficient. No interventional experiment (e.g., training the same base model with/without shared experts or dense layers) is provided; causal language ('dense modules may interfere...') remains conjecture.

Some high-SRP models owe their scores to expert imbalance (LLaMA-MoE-v2, Yuan2.0, PowerMoE), meaning the headline ranking partly reflects load imbalance rather than genuine segment-level routing structure; while acknowledged, the practical desirability of such 'consistency' for offloading is questionable.

Scale and recency limitations: the analysis caps at 57B parameters and omits the largest current frontier MoE models, and some findings (e.g., effect of shared experts) may not generalize to much larger or differently trained models.

Novelty is moderate: expert activation locality has been previously observed; the contribution is a systematic quantification plus a cache-optimality metric. SRP/SCH are somewhat corpus-dependent oracle upper bounds (best-possible F1/hit rate), so their absolute values are harder to interpret than relative comparisons.

Presentation issues: several main-text figures (Figures 2, 3, 5) are cluttered with 20 models and small markers/labels and are hard to read; Figure 1's SRPE values are not defined for the reader at that point; Table 1's justification for grouping boundaries is loose. Some claims (e.g., transitivity of consistency across domains in E.5) are only supported visually via heatmaps.

The proposed 'segment router' framework is not actually implemented or evaluated as a method (e.g., no demonstration that segment-level routing approximates model quality), limiting the significance of the SRP metric beyond a diagnostic.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly defined metrics (SRP, SCH, ρ) for quantifying local routing consistency, with formal derivations and proofs in the appendix showing the metrics are intrinsic, method-independent properties

Broad empirical scope: 20 MoE LLMs across 3B–57B parameters and diverse architectures, with careful setup details (corpora construction, base vs. post-trained comparisons, position-independence checks, statistical confidence intervals via bootstrapping)

Practically relevant findings: identifying architectural factors (MoE on every layer, no shared experts) correlated with higher consistency, the domain vs. vocabulary specialization analysis, and the actionable ρ=2 cache-size guideline

Sensible validation of the oracle metric: SCH is shown to be highly correlated with hit rates of practical caching algorithms (LRU/LFU/Fixed) and with SRP, mitigating concerns about oracle-based upper bounds
Strong reproducibility commitment: deterministic corpus construction, code release, and detailed appendix (model configs, data processing)
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the metrics are essentially cleverly framed variants of best-case F1/recall on segment-level expert activation counts; the analysis is confirmatory of already-reported locality phenomena (e.g., Mixtral consecutive activation), extended to more models and longer segments

No end-to-end system evaluation: the paper never implements an actual expert-offloading pipeline to validate that SRP/SCH differences translate into real speedups or that the ρ=2 recommendation improves wall-clock latency; all claims are proxy-based

Causal claims are not supported: the conclusion that dense modules (dense layers/shared experts) 'interfere or weaken MoE routing signals' is a conjecture from correlational table comparisons across confounded architectures (training data, tokenizer, scale, objective all differ); no controlled or interventional experiments (e.g., ablating shared experts in one model family)

Confounded model comparisons: group-level conclusions about architecture are drawn from only ~20 heterogeneous models with widely varying training recipes; LLaMA-MoE-v2's top SRP is driven by constantly-activated experts (load imbalance), suggesting the metric conflates consistency with degenerate routing, and the interpretation of 'high SRP' is not always aligned with deployment desirability

Evaluation corpora are English-centric generic text plus a few instruction datasets; encoder-decoder translation models (NLLB) are evaluated on non-translation inputs, making their low scores difficult to interpret; tokenization differences across models further complicate cross-model comparisons

Figures 2, 4, 6 are cluttered scatter plots with many overlapping labeled points that are hard to read; several key claims (e.g., 'turning points near ρ=2') rely on visual inspection rather than quantitative characterization

The significance of the contribution relative to the venue is modest: this is an empirical measurement study without a new method, system, or theory; the actionable output (a heuristic cache-size rule) is thin for a top-tier AI conference

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated research question: whether MoE architectures differ in 'local routing consistency' is practically important for expert offloading on memory-constrained devices, and prior work (e.g., Mixtral consecutive-activation observations, LRU-based offloading) only examined single models or very short spans.

Two carefully defined, formally grounded metrics (SRP and SCH) with complete derivations in the appendix; the oracle/best-achievable formulation makes the metrics method-agnostic, and the correlation analysis between SRP, SCH, and real cache algorithms (LRU/LFU/Fixed) supports their practical relevance.

Impressive breadth of empirical analysis: 20 MoE LLMs spanning 3B–57B parameters and diverse architectures, a multi-domain corpus combining RedPajama and downstream application data, and extensive supporting analyses (base vs. post-trained comparison, position-wise stability, domain transferability, confidence intervals via bootstrapping, layer-wise and expert-level breakdowns).

Actionable and reasonably supported findings: the association of high consistency with per-layer MoE and absence of shared experts, the role of domain- vs. vocabulary-specialized experts, and the ~2x active-expert cache size recommendation provide concrete guidance for both model designers and offloading system builders.
Good reproducibility posture: deterministic corpus construction, promised release of the sampled corpus and source code, and detailed model/data configuration in the appendix.
weaknesses: The study is purely observational. No end-to-end validation is provided that the proposed metrics actually predict real offloading performance (e.g., latency, throughput, or output quality under an actual offloading system). Correlation with cache hit rates is a proxy; a demonstration with a real system (e.g., an offloading framework with LRU/SwapMoE-style policies) would substantially strengthen the central claims.

The '2x active experts' cache size recommendation is derived from turning points of an oracle (best-achievable) hit-rate curve; real cache policies without oracle knowledge may not exhibit the same optimum, so the practical applicability of this conclusion is unverified.

Some high-SRP models achieve their scores largely via always-active / highly imbalanced experts (e.g., LLaMA-MoE-v2 with LB 29.04, PowerMoE), which arguably conflates expert imbalance with genuine routing consistency; the paper acknowledges this but the metric design does not disentangle the two, weakening the model ranking conclusions.

The architectural conclusions ('MoE on every layer' and 'no shared experts' cause high consistency) are correlational over 20 heterogeneous models with many confounds (training data, tokenizer, size, training recipe). No controlled experiment (e.g., training small MoEs with/without shared experts) is performed, so causal language in places exceeds the evidence.

Novelty is moderate: the core idea (consecutive expert activation locality enabling caching) is already known and exploited in prior systems; the contribution is mainly systematization and quantification rather than a new method, which limits impact for a top-tier venue.

Minor presentation issues: the abstract text appears truncated, Equation 8's denominator has a notation error (Σ_{e=E} instead of Σ_{e∈E}), and some figures (e.g., Figure 2, Figure 4) are cluttered with overlapping labels and hard to read.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper identifies that local routing consistency (locality of expert activations) varies across MoE models and directly determines the feasibility of expert offloading, a property that prior work only observed anecdotally on single models (e.g., Mixtral) over short spans.

Two complementary and carefully defined metrics: SRP (parameter-free, intrinsic to the expert/model, with a formal proof that the optimal segment estimator is a thresholded activation-frequency rule) and SCH (an oracle cache metric with a hard cache limit that bridges analysis and real offloading systems). The connection to the clairvoyant (Belady) replacement policy is appropriate.

Broad and convincing empirical scope: 20 real MoE LLMs spanning 3B–57B and diverse architectures (dense-interleaved, shared experts, encoder-decoder, SSM-hybrid), plus a set of ~1.4B toy models pretrained from scratch to isolate causal factors (load-balance loss coefficient, shared experts, expert count/granularity). The REAL+TOY design strengthens the causal claims beyond pure correlation.

The findings are informative and actionable: a trade-off between local routing consistency and local load balance, while global load balance can coexist with high consistency via domain-specialized experts; shared experts and restricted expert combination space harm consistency; domain specialization matters more than vocabulary specialization; high SCH correlates strongly (r ≈ 0.9+) with LRU/LFU hit rates. These are useful guidelines for both MoE architecture design and offloading system design.

Good thoroughness in supporting analysis: position-wise and layer-wise SRP stability, base vs. post-trained comparisons, bootstrapped confidence intervals, SRP–SCH correlation tables, and a released corpus/code with a reproducibility statement.
weaknesses: The practical significance is under-validated end-to-end. The throughput experiment (Appendix F) shows only weak correlations between SCH and relative overhead of a naive LRU offloading system (r ≈ 0.2 prefill, r ≈ −0.3 decoding), which the authors themselves acknowledge. The headline claims about offloading friendliness therefore rest mostly on proxy metrics rather than demonstrated speedups on a real system.

The central deployment recommendation (cache size ≈ 2x active experts balances effectiveness and efficiency) is loosely supported: only group-1 models exhibit clear SCH turning points near ρ = 2, and the 'efficiency' side of the trade-off is never formally modeled (memory cost is trivially linear in ρ, so the argument is essentially 'diminishing returns of SCH'), making the 2x rule feel more empirical heuristic than derived conclusion.

Some findings are relatively expected: the load-balance vs. locality trade-off, and the argument that shared experts reduce the expert combination space, are intuitive and partially anticipated by prior work (e.g., Muennighoff et al. on OLMoE); the paper's contribution here is confirmation at scale rather than conceptual novelty.

All metrics are computed on human-authored prefill-like text, while the primary claimed benefit is the autoregressive decoding stage, where future tokens are model-generated and routing statistics may differ; this distribution mismatch is only partially addressed by the informal Appendix F analysis.

Toy-model conclusions rest on a single scale (1.43B OLMoE-like) and single data mixture; effects of shared experts or combination space at larger scales or with different data remain unverified. Also, attribution of low SRP in real models to specific architectural causes (vs. confounds like training data or scale) is necessarily speculative for groups 3–4.

Presentation issues: several figures (e.g., Figures 4, 6, 7) are dense with 20 overlaid models and hard to read; there are typos and grammar errors ('explanable', 'specialzations', 'Shared experts harms'); and the abstract's claim of 'optimal balance' is stronger than the evidence warrants.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and underexplored question: to what degree MoE LLMs exhibit local routing consistency that can be exploited by expert offloading systems.
The proposed metrics (SRP and SCH) are formally defined, with derivations and proofs in the appendix, and are designed to be model-intrinsic rather than tied to a specific offloading implementation.

The empirical coverage is broad: 20 MoE LLMs spanning 3B-54B parameters and diverse architectures (dense-interleaved, shared experts, encoder-decoder, hybrid SSM), plus a set of controlled toy models trained from scratch to isolate causal factors (load balance loss, shared experts, expert granularity, expert combination space).

The findings are useful for the community: the trade-off between local routing consistency and local load balance, the negative effect of shared experts, the distinction between domain and vocabulary specialization, and the empirical validation that SCH correlates with real cache algorithms (LRU/LFU) and the clairvoyant optimum.
The authors commit to releasing code and the sampled corpus, and report confidence intervals via bootstrapping, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty in the core contribution: the paper is primarily an observational/empirical study. The phenomenon of expert activation locality was already noted (Jiang et al. 2024; Eliseev & Mazur 2023; Xue et al. 2024b), and the main advance is a systematic quantification rather than a fundamentally new insight or method.

The headline practical takeaway (cache size ~2x the number of active experts) is a weak, heuristic result derived from visual inspection of SCH curves ('turning points near rho = 2') rather than from a principled analysis or cost model, and its generality across architectures and deployment settings is unclear.

The connection to real system performance is underdeveloped. The only end-to-end validation (Appendix F) uses a naive LRU-based implementation on toy models and reports weak correlations (r ~ -0.3 during decoding, ~0.2 during prefill), which the authors themselves acknowledge leaves throughput largely unexplained by local routing consistency. No benchmark against modern offloading systems (Pre-gated MoE, Fiddler, MoE-Infinity) is provided.

The corpus is limited to 512-token samples, which constrains conclusions about long-context behavior, where topic shifts and cache pressure are most relevant to expert offloading; results on segment position and domain effects are only shown for this fixed length.

Several findings are confirmatory of intuition (imbalanced routing yields higher consistency; shared experts and reduced combination space reduce consistency), and the toy-model analysis, while controlled, relies on 1.4B-scale models trained for only 10K steps, so conclusions may not transfer to production-scale training.

Some metric design choices are debatable: SRP's reliance on a thresholded F1 optimum with a specific segment-prediction constraint is somewhat contrived, and the choice of segment length m is left as a free parameter whose sensitivity is discussed but not resolved; the added value of SRP over the simpler SCH is partially redundant given their near-perfect correlation.

Writing and presentation issues: Figure 1 (emoji-based routing visualization) is unconventional and hard to interpret; several figures (Figures 4, 6, 10-11) are dense and illegible at print scale; a few typographical/grammar issues remain ('Shared experts harms', 'explanable', 'more significant than', 'activate' vs 'activation').

Significance is moderate: the paper informs model design and caching heuristics but does not itself deliver a new architecture, training method, or system, and the actionable guidance for practitioners remains thin.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: quantifying 'local routing consistency' across MoE LLMs to inform expert-offloading design is a relevant and underexplored angle, moving beyond anecdotal observations (e.g., Mixtral's 2-token locality) to a systematic study.

Two complementary, well-defined metrics: SRP is a parameter-free, intrinsic property of experts with a formal derivation (Appendix C includes proofs that the optimal segment estimator thresholds on activation frequency), while SCH connects the analysis to practical caching with a hard cache limit. The treatment of SRP as an oracle/potential metric and validation against LRU/LFU/clairvoyant baselines is methodologically sound.

Impressively broad empirical coverage: 20 MoE LLMs spanning 3B–57B parameters, diverse architectures (dense-interleaved, shared experts, encoder-decoder, SSM-hybrid), plus a controlled set of toy OLMoE-style models pretrained from scratch to isolate causal factors (load balance coefficient, shared experts, expert granularity, combination space). This combination of observational and interventional evidence is a real strength.

Interesting and actionable findings: the trade-off between local routing consistency and local load balance, the coexistence of consistency with global load balance via domain-specialized experts, the harmful effect of shared experts, and the domain- vs vocabulary-specialization distinction are novel and useful for both architecture design and system deployment.

Good rigor and reproducibility: bootstrap confidence intervals (Table 8), correlation analysis across metrics and cache algorithms (Tables 3, 7), position-invariance and base-vs-post-trained checks, deterministic pipeline, and code/corpus release promises. The appendix throughput analysis (Appendix F) adds a link to real systems.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the paper is a measurement/analysis study. No new training method, routing scheme, caching algorithm, or system is proposed, and no end-to-end demonstration that acting on the findings improves real deployments. The headline conclusions (e.g., 'cache size ≈ 2x active experts') are derived only for the highest-consistency group (group 1) and may not generalize, which somewhat overstates the practical takeaway.

The causal claims rest on small, undertrained toy models (1.43B, only 10k steps on 20B tokens), so conclusions about shared experts and expert combination space could be artifacts of undertraining; no verification at a second scale is provided.

The practical validation is weak: the correlation between SCH and measured throughput of the naive offloading system in Appendix F is modest (r ≈ 0.2 prefilling, r ≈ −0.3 decoding), which the authors themselves acknowledge, yet the abstract/introduction claim the findings 'pave the way for memory-efficient MoE design and deployment without compromising inference speed.'

Both metrics rely on oracle information (optimal segment router / oracle eviction), and while the argument that SCH approximates Belady-optimal behavior is reasonable, the gap between oracle metrics and achievable performance of learned predictors (e.g., prefetchers) is not directly quantified.

Some findings feel incremental or expected (locality benefits caching; shared experts reduce routing flexibility), and the group taxonomies of REAL models are somewhat post-hoc. The paper also restricts attention to FFN-replacing MoE layers, limiting scope.
Presentation issues: several figures (4, 8, 12–13) are dense and hard to read in the main text; key quantitative results are scattered across the appendix, making the main claims harder to verify.
